title: The Seventh Annual General Counsel Report (Part Two): Entering the Unfazed Era
pub: FTI Consulting / Relativity (interviews and analysis by Ari Kaplan Advisors)
author: FTI Technology · Relativity · Ari Kaplan

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The report accepts the cluster’s supervised, task-specific adoption model and materially extends it with current evidence from large corporate legal departments: use is concentrated in bounded document workflows, comfort falls for sensitive tasks, and effective deployment requires human review, structured training, expert support and risk-aware technology roadmaps. It does not directly assess apprenticeship deskilling or lawyer replacement.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The report accepts selective, human-supervised deployment and adds empirical evidence from large corporate legal departments: adoption is concentrated in bounded tasks, comfort varies by use case, review remains important, and value depends on coordinated planning, governance, legal operations and resource allocation rather than indiscriminate tool adoption.

The budget has not changed, but we  have been investing in more tools that will provide  a long-term impact.” To this point, general counsel have largely  maintained a healthy balance of caution and  confidence in pursuing innovation (in many cases,  more enthusiastically than in  years’ past), experimenting  with new tools and allocating  resources between technology,  internal resources and outside  providers.

st.t: AI adoption: Enthusiasm cannot establish investment value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s bounded account: general counsel report use or testing concentrated in specific information-processing tasks, with comfort varying by task. Its qualified endorsement preserves human analysis and highlights privacy, discoverability, security and accuracy concerns; it offers no evidence that enthusiasm or adoption establishes investment value.

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: The report supports the cluster’s proposition by documenting rapid in-house AI adoption alongside persistent organisational-readiness constraints. Its evidence that many departments still lack technology roadmaps, need structured training and expect a stronger legal-operations role reinforces the view that capturing AI gains depends on planning, skills and implementation capacity rather than procurement alone. It does not establish realised productivity, pricing or insourcing effects.
qs: (NYSE: FCN) and legal data intelligence company Relativity, show generative artificial intelligence ("AI") adoption in corporate legal departments has nearly doubled year over year, with 87% of general counsel now reporting use within their teams, compared with 44% in 2025.
This still leaves nearly half of  legal departments without a roadmap to support  digital transformation but demonstrates significant  improvement in only one year’s time.

kp.k: Findings combine interviews with a separate international survey
kp.d: The 2026 report draws on Ari Kaplan's September 2025 interviews with 30 general counsel or chief legal officers: 63% had global responsibilities and 59% worked in organizations exceeding $500 million annual revenue. Separately, Censuswide surveyed 224 general counsel and chief legal officers in summer 2025 at organizations exceeding $100 million annual revenue and 1,000 employees across South America, North America, Europe and Asia Pacific. Technology leaders supplied anecdotal insights. Findings labeled qualitative and quantitative therefore come from distinct evidence streams.
qs: In September 2025, Ari Kaplan conducted personal interviews with 30 leaders serving as general counsel or chief legal officers of their organizations.
He also interviewed technology and digital transformation leaders at global organizations for anecdotal insights into how their responsibilities and views overlap with the general counsel.

kp.k: Reported generative AI adoption rises sharply
kp.d: The qualitative survey reports legal-department generative AI adoption of 20% in the 2023 edition, 28% in 2024, 44% in 2025 and 87% in 2026. Most remaining nonusers planned implementation in the coming year. The report qualifies this expansion by stating that most current use cases remain limited to Copilot, ChatGPT and contracting tools; these are reported adoption findings, not measured productivity outcomes.
qs: Generative AI has become a fixture in the legal department, with 87% of respondents indicating they now use the technology.
This is a substantial increase from the prior year, when 44% said they were using generative AI.
That said, the majority of current use cases are limited to Copilot, ChatGPT and contracting tools.

kp.k: Summarization leads a mixture of experimentation and deployment
kp.d: Qualitative responses combine actual use with testing: summarization 83%, general queries 70%, meeting notes 67%, identifying specific contract clauses 63%, audio and video transcription 53%, foreign-language analysis 40%, first-pass review 37%, searching company knowledge repositories 33% and chronology development 27%. These figures do not distinguish production deployment from experimentation.
qs: FOR WHICH TASKS ARE YOU CURRENTLY USING OR TESTING GENERATIVE AI?
Respondents said the most common task for generative AI was summarization, with 83% either using or experimenting with it.

kp.k: Technology planning expands alongside intended investment
kp.d: Technology roadmaps rose from 25% to 53% in the qualitative survey, leaving nearly half without one. Roughly 70% planned to purchase or expand technologies in the coming year, particularly contract lifecycle management, other contracting tools and AI. The report identifies AI at 39% and non-AI technology at 37% as strategic priorities for efficiency and efficacy. These spending figures describe intentions, not completed investments.
qs: This year, 53% of general counsel said they have a technology roadmap in place, compared to 25% the previous year.
Most indicated their technology investments this year will focus on contract lifecycle management, other contracting technology and various forms of AI.

kp.d: Most departments relied on webinars, conferences, demonstrations and articles to keep pace. Approximately 17% reported formal approaches such as task forces, regular training or legal operations support; 13% reported no technology-upskilling efforts. Interviewees cited workload and time constraints. FTI Technology's Sophie Ross recommends structured training, education, expert support and roadmaps combining innovation with risk mitigation.
qs: Approximately 17% said they have a formalized approach, which included internal task forces, regular training programs or legal operations support to keep the legal team up to date.
Still, 13% of general counsel said they had no efforts in place to upskill their teams for technology advancements.

General counsel will need to provide their departments with structured training, education and expert support to use this technology effectively, and underpin those efforts with technology roadmaps that enable innovation alongside risk mitigation.

kp.k: AI supplements outside expertise amid rising workload
kp.d: The report describes growing legal complexity and capacity pressure rather than replacement of external counsel. Quantitative responses identify outside service providers at 47%, up from 32%; AI/generative AI at 39%, up from 29%; and law firms at 37%, unchanged. Separately, the narrative reports roughly two-thirds relying primarily on outside counsel. One general counsel described using AI for regulatory summaries and updates while checking them against outside counsel's expertise. The source does not classify outside service providers as ALSPs.
qs: Ultimately, general counsel are looking to technology for efficiencies but continue to value trusted relationships and outside expertise.

Historically, we performed most of our legal work internally, but given the issues associated with global trade, we are relying more on outside counsel. Given the complexity of regulations and how quickly they are changing, we also rely on generative AI for summaries and updates, but we check those against the expertise of our outside counsel.

kp.k: Comfort remains task-specific and conditional on human review
kp.d: Respondents expressed greater comfort with research, e-discovery, document review, drafting and contract analysis, and greater discomfort with investigations, breach response, early case assessment and privilege review. One general counsel explicitly conditioned drafting comfort on reviewing the output, treated generative AI as a supplement to discovery workflows and retained human scrutiny for privilege. These are reported attitudes and practices, not evidence of tool accuracy or autonomous reliability.
qs: Use cases that had the highest rate of response for “uncomfortable” included investigations, data breach response, early case assessment and privilege review.
But with privilege review, I want human eyes on the majority of work, at least for now, because it is so critical.
I am still skeptical and human analysis still makes a difference. I am often comfortable with a first pass using generative AI.

kp.k: Legal and technical leaders differ on AI risk
kp.d: Few general counsel ranked AI among their top five risks, but roughly 70% raised concerns in qualitative interviews about effects on departments, businesses, employment and society. Quantitative respondents most frequently selected data privacy, new discoverable evidence and security as generative AI concerns. CIO interviewees instead ranked hallucinations and inaccuracy highest and were generally less comfortable with AI in legal use cases; none reported being extremely comfortable in any listed category.
qs: While few placed AI in the rankings of their top five risks, roughly 70% expressed concerns in qualitative interviews about the impact of AI on their departments, business, employment and society.
In the quantitative survey, data privacy, creation of a new source of discoverable evidence and security were the most frequently selected areas.
These ratings were moderately consistent with those of the CIOs interviewed, who expressed concern across all categories and rated hallucinations and inaccuracy as the top risk area.

kp.k: Agentic AI preparedness remains particularly low
kp.d: On a 1–5 preparedness scale, qualitative-survey weighted averages for general counsel's generative AI readiness rose from 1.85 in 2025 to 2.43 in 2026, versus 2.33 for technology leaders in 2026. Agentic AI scored 1.7 for general counsel and 1.33 for technology leaders; AI video generation scored 1.93 and 1.33 respectively. The report presents these as perceived readiness and suggests possible room for stronger cross-functional collaboration.
qs: On a scale from 1-5, with 1 being “not prepared at all” and 5 being “very prepared,” how prepared are companies to handle the following issues?
To some extent, these leaders are the most worried about different things, which could suggest room for improvement in cross-functional collaboration.

kp.k: AI regulation adds to compliance-monitoring demands
kp.d: The quantitative survey reports monitoring of the EU AI Act by 47% in 2026 versus 35% in 2025; AI regulation in the EU or other non-U.S. jurisdictions by 37% versus 35%; and U.S. federal or state AI regulation by 37% versus 21%. Interviewees described difficulty keeping pace with regulations and the need to exploit AI opportunities without creating undue risk.
qs: What worries me most at the moment is the vast volume of new regulations, including those related to the governance of AI.

Increasingly, AI is being viewed as the panacea for driving efficiencies; however, there are associated data risks, and the potential impact on employees is a crucial consideration. We are also being inundated with regulations, so it is difficult to keep up.

kp.k: AI artifacts are expected to expand discovery obligations
kp.d: All participating CIOs and 80% of general counsel expected AI outputs, logs and prompts to come within litigation and investigations. This is an expectation rather than a measured increase in discovery activity: one general counsel explicitly said they had not yet seen the issue. Another warned that people rely on convenient AI tools without critically reviewing generated material.
qs: Additionally, respondents discussed the consideration of AI artifacts as a new form of emerging data, as AI outputs, logs and prompts may begin to come into scope in litigation and investigations.
All CIO participants said they expect this to happen and 80% of general counsel agreed.
I think this will be a mess. I have not seen it, but I expect it to be an issue.
People are not reviewing AI-generated content with a critical eye.

kp.k: Legal operations grows as technology adoption support
kp.d: Dedicated legal operations functions increased from 29% in 2025 to 41% in 2026 in the qualitative survey, although fewer than half had one. Departments without dedicated staff cited budget or lack of need. The report suggests some leaders may not understand the function's value or optimal structure. One general counsel predicted an enhanced role as generative AI grows and characterized legal operations leaders as technology ambassadors.
qs: For those who do not, there continues to be a mix of reasons, with many noting that their department lacks the budget or need for a dedicated operations employee.

We expect to enhance this role, especially with the emergence of generative AI. As technology becomes more important, legal operations become more important. Legal operations leaders are the department's ambassadors to legal technology.

kp.k: Data capabilities influence provider use and lawyer recruitment
kp.d: Qualitative responses identify outside providers supporting knowledge management and data governance at 38%, providers enabling data-driven insights at 31%, recruitment of lawyers experienced in enabling and acting on such insights at 28%, and recruitment for data governance skills at 21%. Interviewees linked these capabilities to doing more with less and improving internal and provider decisions; one described desired outside-counsel analysis of employment-dispute drivers as not yet happening.
qs: The company's focus is on doing more with less, and having professionals or outside providers who can interpret data helps us identify potential advantages and gaps.
I wish we were tasking our outside counsel with better analyzing the data that we generate with them to provide insights about our primary drivers of employment disputes, for example, but we are not.
Given modern litigation, I would not hire someone without good data governance skills, which are crucial.

kp.k: Workforce transformation is anticipated rather than demonstrated
kp.d: The report's conclusion interprets general counsel as balancing caution and confidence while allocating resources among technology, internal teams and outside providers. An unnamed legal leader predicts a very different legal workforce within two years, but the statement supplies no staffing numbers or specific displacement mechanism. Relativity's David Horrigan similarly frames increased adoption as the end of the 'Luddite Lawyer' and emergence of the 'TechnoLawyer'; this is his interpretation of the reported adoption trends.
qs: In the next two years, the legal workforce will look very different.
The 2026 edition of The General Counsel Report is significant because it provides compelling evidence indicating the era of the 'Luddite Lawyer' is over

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The report claims generative AI has become routine in the surveyed corporate legal departments, with adoption rising sharply and further implementation planned.
pts.d: The report gives adoption figures of 20% in its 2023 edition, 28% in 2024, 44% in 2025 and 87% in 2026. These are reported-use measures, not measures of deployment intensity or effectiveness. It qualifies the breadth of adoption by stating that most current use cases are limited to Copilot, ChatGPT and contracting tools. Most remaining non-users reportedly plan implementation during the coming year. Relativity's David Horrigan interprets this trajectory as the end of the 'Luddite Lawyer' era and the emergence of a 'TechnoLawyer'; that is his interpretation of adoption and interview findings, not a separately measured professional transformation.

pts.k: The report presents AI as a growing response to legal workload and capacity constraints, alongside—not demonstrably replacing—outside expertise.
pts.d: In the quantitative survey, 39% selected AI/generative AI as a strategy for increased work and risk, compared with 29% previously; the report also describes the 39% as prioritizing AI for efficiency and efficacy. The corresponding European figure for addressing capacity constraints is 53%. An interviewed general counsel describes using AI for regulatory summaries and updates while checking them against outside counsel's expertise. These findings establish reported strategies and experiences, not measured savings, reduced headcount or displacement of law firms. The narrative reports roughly two-thirds relying primarily on outside counsel, whereas the quantitative strategy table gives 37% selecting law firms; these figures should not be treated as the same measure.

pts.k: AI is being used or tested predominantly for summarization and supporting tasks, with interviewed counsel describing human-reviewed augmentation rather than autonomous legal work.
pts.d: The qualitative cohort reports using or testing AI for summarization (83%), general queries (70%), meeting notes (67%), identifying contract clauses (63%), audio/video transcription (53%), foreign-language material analysis (40%) and first-pass review (37%). The report describes comfort with research, discovery, document review and contracting, but greater reservations about investigations, data-breach response, early case assessment and privilege review. One general counsel conditions comfort with drafting on human review and treats generative AI as a supplement to discovery workflows. These are usage and attitude findings, not task-performance benchmarks.

pts.k: The report and named executive commentary argue that growing AI use makes structured training, technology planning and legal operations more important.
pts.d: FTI Technology CEO Sophie Ross says effective AI use will require structured training, education, expert support and technology roadmaps balancing innovation with risk mitigation. The report finds only approximately 17% of interviewed counsel have formalized technology-upskilling approaches and 13% have none. Technology roadmaps increased from 25% to 53%, while roughly 70% plan technology purchases or expansion; those figures cover technology generally, not AI alone. An unnamed general counsel predicts an enhanced legal operations role as generative AI and technology become more important. The observed increase in dedicated legal operations functions, from 29% to 41%, is not established as caused by AI.

pts.k: Interviewees predict that AI artifacts will become evidence in litigation and investigations, creating substantial discovery implications.
pts.d: The report says all interviewed CIO participants and 80% of interviewed general counsel expect AI outputs, logs and prompts to come into scope in litigation and investigations. Unnamed counsel anticipate a 'mess' and a 'huge' e-discovery impact. One explicitly states that they have not yet seen the issue, marking the statement as a forecast rather than a reported incident. Another connects the concern to people relying on AI-generated content without critical review. No volume, cost estimate or date is supplied.

pts.k: Interviewees identify additional AI-related governance risks and predict workforce change, but do not specify a displacement trajectory.
pts.d: Roughly 70% of the qualitative cohort expressed concerns about AI's effects on departments, business, employment and society. A general counsel cautions that efficiency expectations coexist with data risks and potential employee impacts; a CIO warns about company data connecting to public AI. In the quantitative survey, leading concerns include privacy (25%), new discoverable evidence/discovery response (24%) and security (24%); job loss or obsolete skillsets is a reported concern at 21%, not an observed employment outcome. The conclusion quotes an unnamed legal leader predicting that the legal workforce will look very different within two years, without specifying roles, direction, scale or mechanism.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of two distinct respondent studies, anecdotal technology-leader interviews and executive interpretation—not performance testing or demonstrated market outcomes.
pts.d: Ari Kaplan interviewed 30 general counsel/CLOs in September 2025; 63% had global responsibilities and 59% worked at organizations with over $500 million in annual revenue. Separately, Censuswide surveyed 224 general counsel/CLOs in summer 2025 at organizations exceeding $100 million in revenue and 1,000 employees across four regions. Technology and transformation leaders supplied anecdotal perspectives; their number is not stated. The report labels adoption, task use, roadmaps, comfort and legal operations figures as based on its qualitative survey, while strategy and main-concern figures come from the quantitative survey. Prior editions provide the year-over-year comparisons, but the supplied methodology does not establish a matched longitudinal panel. Claims about efficiency and workforce transformation are supported by reported intentions, experience or expectation, not measured productivity, staffing effects, benchmarks or legal cases. Some extracted chart values and labels are internally inconsistent, so individual chart cells should not be used to infer precision beyond the clear narrative and labels.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The 2026 publication reports 2025 fieldwork; forward-looking claims concern the coming year or an unspecified two-year horizon and are qualified by training, review and risk controls.
pts.d: The launch release is dated 11 March 2026, but interviews occurred in September 2025 and the quantitative survey in summer 2025. Accordingly, the '2026' adoption figure denotes the report edition rather than a March 2026 measurement. The release frames planned technology investment as the next 12 months; the report describes remaining AI implementation plans as the coming year. The unnamed workforce forecast says 'the next two years' without fixing whether the reference point is interview or publication. Discovery-artifact predictions have no specific deadline. Effective deployment is expressly conditioned on upskilling, governance and human verification; willingness to use AI varies by task and familiarity. Agentic AI readiness remains low in self-ratings—1.7/5 for counsel and 1.33/5 for technology leaders—rather than being evidence of widespread autonomous deployment.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims primarily concern large-company legal buyers and their teams, with implications for legal operations, technology leadership, outside counsel and discovery professionals.
pts.d: General counsel/CLOs are portrayed as adopting AI to handle demand, setting technology strategy and overseeing associated risks. In-house lawyers face greater expectations to learn tools and verify outputs. Legal operations professionals are expected by an interviewee to take a stronger technology-enablement role. CIOs and transformation leaders confront cross-functional governance and security issues and report more cautious attitudes toward legal AI use. Outside counsel and service providers remain sources of expertise, verification and additional capacity; the report does not establish AI-driven provider displacement or identify outside providers collectively as ALSPs. Litigation, investigation and information-governance teams may need to manage new AI-generated evidence. Broader employment and societal effects appear as concerns, while the source offers no specific findings on small firms, consumer legal services or access to justice.
